what: The five synthetic readers of the first study, on release candidate 2. Every one is invented: the names, the lives and every word attributed to them. They describe a situation and a question, so anybody can argue with them; none models a real person or a composite of real people. Chosen by Dinis's brief of 19 October 2026: two from Generation Z and two from Generation X, the book's two readers under the Gen ZX frame (decision 015), and one publisher who decides whether to commission the book under their imprint.
why_these: Generation Z, two ways in: one who already codes with agents and wants a company, and one who has never coded and has an idea. Chapter 8 says both are developers; this tests whether the book convinces the second.

Generation X, two ways in: the expert founder the frame is written for, and the sceptic who will probably never buy, who reads adversarially and finds the claims that do not hold. The newsroom's method says to include one every time.

The publisher, because the book's next question after rc2 is whether it is the kind of thing somebody would put their name and money behind, and because a publisher reads a manuscript as a proposal, a sample and a skim, which is a different path from any reader's.
One on a phone: Aisha reads on a phone in short sessions, which is where patience runs out first.
not_the_cast: The storyboard cast (Zara, Tomás, Priya, Sam, and Marta proposed) are characters in the book's story; these are readers of the book, records with a situation and a question. The nearest cast member is named for each, so the two can be compared.

personas.name: Aisha Bello
personas.situation: Final-year computer science student in Manchester. Uses coding agents every day for coursework and a side project, a revision app with about 200 users from her course. Has two graduate job offers she is lukewarm about, and a friend asking her to start something together after graduation.
personas.arrives_with: Should I take the job or start the company, and does this book tell me how to actually do the second?
personas.knows: Coding with agents, prompting, GitHub, deploying a web app, what vibe coding means online.
personas.does_not_know: What forming a company involves, pricing, selling, funding without investors, who Dinis Cruz is, what Wardley maps are, what SG/Send, sgit or RiskMandate are.
personas.decides_on: Whether a friend she trusts says it is good, and whether the first chapter talks to her rather than at her.
personas.leaves_when: She is lectured, given history she did not ask for, or reads the same point twice. Hustle-culture tone also loses her.
personas.patience: low: reads on her phone in ten-minute bursts on the bus; skims anything that does not earn the next screen
personas.format: phone, in the browser or an ebook app
personas.reads_like: Skims headings, reads openings and endings of chapters, stops at lists and anything she could act on today.

personas.name: Ellie Marsh
personas.situation: Account manager at a small marketing agency in Bristol. Has never written code. Uses ChatGPT for drafts at work. Has an idea she has been sitting on for a year: a booking and reminders tool for independent dog groomers, because her sister is one and runs the business from a paper diary and WhatsApp.
personas.arrives_with: Can someone like me, who has never coded, actually build and sell this, and will this book show me how without making me feel stupid?
personas.knows: Marketing, customers, how small businesses buy, social media, using a chat assistant.
personas.does_not_know: What an agent is beyond a chat window, servers, databases, serverless, graphs, open source, what a repository is.
personas.decides_on: Whether it feels written for her, whether there is something she can do this weekend, and the reviews.
personas.leaves_when: Jargon piles up without explanation, it assumes she codes, or it turns out to be a book about the author's products.
personas.patience: medium: reads in the evening on her Kindle, a chapter at a time; will push through one hard chapter, not two in a row
personas.reads_like: Reads in order, every word of a chapter that speaks to her, skims the ones that do not, highlights lines to come back to.

personas.name: Nadia Rahman
personas.situation: Twenty-two years in insurance claims operations in Leeds, now head of claims operations at a mid-sized insurer. Has described the same triage tool to three vendors and two internal IT projects; none was built. Has savings, a mortgage nearly paid, a daughter at university (Generation Z) who keeps telling her to just build it with AI. Has used ChatGPT, never an agent.
personas.arrives_with: At 51, with no coding, can I really build the first version of this myself, and what would it take to leave my job and run it as a company?
personas.knows: Her domain deeply, buyers in insurance, procurement, regulation (FCA), budgets, managing teams, how vendors sell.
personas.does_not_know: How agents work, what serverless means, how to form or fund a company, what explorer coding or a graph of ideas is.
personas.decides_on: Whether the author has done it and shows it, whether the steps are concrete, whether it respects her experience.
personas.leaves_when: It talks down to her generation, it is vague where she needs specifics, or it is more about the author than about her.
personas.patience: high, but she hates waffle: reads every chapter she starts, and judges hard
personas.reads_like: Reads in order, underlines, writes questions in the margin, checks claims against what she knows of her own industry.

personas.name: Martin Kowalski
personas.situation: Former engineering director at a fintech that was acquired; eight months between roles, doing a little consulting, deciding whether to start something. Thirty years of software. Has read most of the startup canon and several AI books this year, and found most of the AI ones thin. Uses coding agents and is impressed and wary in equal measure.
personas.arrives_with: Is this anything I have not read already, and is it actually a person's thinking or AI slop with a famous-ish name on it?
personas.knows: Software engineering, security basics, cloud, startups from the inside, hiring, vendor lock-in, what a well-made technical book looks like.
personas.does_not_know: The author's newsroom, SG/Send, sgit or RiskMandate, the book's making process beyond what it says.
personas.decides_on: Whether it says something true he has not read before, whether the claims are sourced, and whether it is selling him something.
personas.leaves_when: He catches it padding, repeating itself, selling the author's products, or claiming more than it shows. He will probably not buy; he reads to find the weak points.
personas.patience: medium, adversarial: reads the opening closely, then hunts, skipping to the chapters that make the biggest claims
personas.format: ebook on a tablet, with search
personas.reads_like: Reads like a reviewer: opening, contents, the boldest chapters, the sources, then the end.

personas.name: Catherine Doyle
personas.situation: Publisher at Fernhill Press (invented), an independent UK publisher of business and technology books, about 30 titles a year, sold through bookshops, Amazon and corporate bulk orders. Has commissioned two books on AI in the last year; one sold well, one did not. Was sent the manuscript of release candidate 2 with a note asking whether Fernhill would publish it.
personas.arrives_with: Is there a book here I can sell, to whom, and would I put the Fernhill name on it as it stands or after what changes?
personas.knows: The market for business and technology books, positioning, titles, lengths, what sells to founders, what dates, contracts, rights, what a free online edition does to sales, legal review.
personas.does_not_know: The author's work beyond what the manuscript says, the sgit products, the technical details of agents (she relies on the manuscript to make them clear).
personas.decides_on: Market and audience, the hook in the first pages, the author's platform, timeliness and shelf life, length and structure, risk.
personas.leaves_when: Not applicable: she reads as a commissioning publisher, the front matter and the first chapters closely, then samples and skims to judge the whole, and decides.
personas.patience: professional: reads the first fifty pages properly, then samples every part
personas.reads_like: Proposal first (the front matter and chapter 1), the contents, the first part, then a chapter from each part, then the end.
